solution: The chapter states this directly in Section 3.5(a), *Electronic Configurations in Periods*: the period indicates the value of \(n\) for the outermost or valence shell, and each successive period is associated with the filling of the next higher principal energy level (\(n = 1\), \(n = 2\), and so on). The first period (\(n = 1\)) fills the \(1s\) level and holds two elements; the second period (\(n = 2\)) begins at lithium; the third (\(n = 3\)) begins at sodium; the fourth (\(n = 4\)) begins at potassium. So the period number IS the principal quantum number of the valence shell. The other quantities do not behave this way: the atomic number rises steadily right through the table and does not restart at a period boundary, and the chapter notes that the properties of an element have a periodic dependence on atomic number and **not** on relative atomic mass; while the azimuthal quantum number \(l\) is what the *block* indicates (the subshell last receiving electrons), not the period.

The statement that the \(d\)-block has 8 columns because a \(d\)-subshell holds a maximum of 8 electrons is the incorrect one, and the chapter contradicts it twice over. Section 3.6.3 defines the \(d\)-Block Elements as *the elements of Group 3 to 12* — which is \(12 - 3 + 1 = 10\) columns, exactly as Fig. 3.3 draws them — and gives their general outer electronic configuration as \((n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}\), so the \(d\)-subshell accommodates up to 10 electrons, not 8. This also follows from the orbital count: a \(d\)-subshell has 5 orbitals and each holds 2 electrons, giving \(5 \times 2 = 10\).

The three remaining statements are all sound. Section 3.6.2 puts the \(p\)-Block at Group 13 to 18, i.e. 6 columns, matching the 3 \(p\)-orbitals \(\times\) 2 electrons \(= 6\); the general rule that a block has as many columns as its subshell has electrons holds throughout (\(s\): 2, \(p\): 6, \(d\): 10, \(f\): 14); and the chapter classifies the elements into \(s\)-, \(p\)-, \(d\)- and \(f\)-blocks precisely by *the type of atomic orbitals that are being filled*, which is what the azimuthal quantum number \(l\) labels.

Nuclear mass is the factor that does not affect the valence shell. The chapter identifies the other three explicitly as governing valence electrons. The valence principal quantum number \(n\) fixes how far the outermost shell lies from the nucleus — Section 3.7.1(a) explains that as we descend a group \(n\) increases, the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and the atomic size grows. The nuclear charge \(Z\) sets the attraction pulling those electrons in: across a period the increasing nuclear charge outweighs the shielding, so the outermost electrons are held more and more tightly. And the core electrons matter through *shielding* or *screening* — Section 3.7.1(c) says the effective nuclear charge experienced by a valence electron is less than the actual nuclear charge because of shielding by the intervening core electrons, giving the \(2s\) electron of lithium as the worked example.

Nuclear mass appears nowhere in that account. Consistently with this, the chapter concludes Section 3.5(b) with the statement that the properties of an element have a periodic dependence upon its atomic number and **not** on relative atomic mass — mass changes the nucleus without changing the charge the valence electrons feel.

Nuclear charge is the factor. Section 3.7.1(b) introduces \(\text{O}^{2-}\), \(\text{F}^-\), \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) as isoelectronic species and says of them, in these words, that their radii would be different **because of their different nuclear charges**; the solution to Problem 3.5 sharpens it to a rule — among isoelectronic species, the one with the larger positive nuclear charge will have the smaller radius. Here all three species carry 10 electrons while \(Z = 9\) for \(\text{F}^-\), \(Z = 10\) for \(\text{Ne}\) and \(Z = 11\) for \(\text{Na}^+\), so the same 10 electrons are pulled in progressively harder and the size falls in the order \(\text{F}^- > \text{Ne} > \text{Na}^+\).

That ordering also settles the alternatives. Their sizes are demonstrably **not** the same, so "none of the factors" fails. The valence principal quantum number is \(n = 2\) for all three, so it cannot distinguish them. And since all three have the identical \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) arrangement, the electron-electron repulsion in the outer orbitals is essentially the same in each — it is the varying nuclear charge, and only that, which changes across the set.

The incorrect statement is the one claiming that an electron is more easily removed from an orbital of lower \(n\) than from one of higher \(n\). The truth runs the other way, and the chapter says so: in Section 3.7.1(c) it explains that as we go down a group the outermost electron is increasingly farther from the nucleus and increasingly shielded, so that *the removal of the outermost electron requires less energy down a group* — and going down a group is precisely what raises \(n\). Fig. 3.6(b) measures it: \(\Delta_i H\) falls from \(520\) for \(\text{Li}\) to \(496\), \(419\), \(403\) and \(374\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) for \(\text{Na}\), \(\text{K}\), \(\text{Rb}\) and \(\text{Cs}\). An electron in a lower-\(n\) orbital sits closer to the nucleus and is less shielded, so it is **harder**, not easier, to pull away.

The other three statements hold. The chapter states that the second ionization enthalpy is higher than the first because it is harder to remove an electron from a positively charged ion than from a neutral atom, *and in the same way the third will be higher than the second and so on* — so the value does rise with each successive electron. Fig. 3.5 shows the maxima falling on the noble gases, which the chapter attributes to their closed shells and very stable configurations; breaking into that core noble-gas arrangement therefore costs the largest jump of all, and that jump is exactly what marks the point at which the valence electrons have run out.

Section 3.6.2 gives the two trends needed: non-metallic character increases from left to right across a period, and metallic character increases down a group. Section 3.7.1(e) then supplies a number for it, stating that electronegativity is inversely related to the metallic properties of elements — so the least electronegative element is the most metallic.

Read off the positions: \(\text{B}\) is in Group 13 of Period 2; \(\text{Al}\) sits directly below it in Period 3 and so is more metallic; \(\text{Mg}\) lies to the left of \(\text{Al}\) in the same period, more metallic again; and \(\text{K}\) is further left still (Group 1) and one period lower, making it the most metallic of the four. The chapter's own electronegativity values confirm the sequence exactly — \(\text{K}\ 0.8\) from Table 3.8(b), and \(\text{Mg}\ 1.2\), \(\text{Al}\ 1.5\), \(\text{B}\ 2.0\) from Table 3.8(a). Reversing that rising electronegativity gives the metallic order \(\text{K} > \text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{B}\). Every alternative ordering places boron or aluminium above potassium, which contradicts both trends at once.

Section 3.7.1(e) states that electronegativity is directly related to the non-metallic properties of elements, so the elements rank in non-metallic character exactly as they rank in electronegativity. Table 3.8(a) prints the values: \(\text{F}\ 4.0\), \(\text{N}\ 3.0\), \(\text{C}\ 2.5\) and \(\text{B}\ 2.0\) across Period II, and \(\text{Si}\ 1.8\) in Period III. That gives

\(\text{F}\,(4.0) > \text{N}\,(3.0) > \text{C}\,(2.5) > \text{B}\,(2.0) > \text{Si}\,(1.8)\)

and the same order follows from the positions alone: fluorine, nitrogen, carbon and boron lie right-to-left across Period 2 so their non-metallic character falls in that order, and silicon sits directly below carbon, one period down, where electronegativity has decreased. The point worth being careful about is silicon against boron: silicon is placed **last**, below boron, because \(1.8 < 2.0\). Any ordering that puts silicon ahead of boron reverses the printed values, and any ordering that opens with boron inverts the whole period trend.

The required order is \(\text{F} > \text{O} > \text{Cl} > \text{N}\). Section 3.7.3 notes that the reducing and oxidizing behaviour of the elements is taken up in a later unit, so this chapter does not tabulate oxidizing power itself; what it does give is the underlying property. An oxidizing agent gains electrons, and Section 3.7.1(e) defines electronegativity as the ability of an atom to attract shared electrons to itself, adding that it is directly related to non-metallic character and that non-metallic elements have a strong tendency to gain electrons.

Table 3.8(a) prints \(\text{F}\ 4.0\), \(\text{O}\ 3.5\) and \(\text{N}\ 3.0\) across Period II and \(\text{Cl}\ 3.0\) in Period III. Fluorine, the most electronegative element in the whole table, must come first and oxygen second; any sequence placing oxygen or chlorine ahead of fluorine, or chlorine ahead of oxygen, contradicts these printed values. Chlorine and nitrogen are both listed at \(3.0\), so the electronegativity table alone does not separate them — but the chapter's other evidence does. Table 3.7 gives chlorine the most negative electron gain enthalpy of any element listed, \(-349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), and Section 3.7.3 identifies the halogens at the extreme right as showing maximum reactivity by the gain of an electron to form an anion; a Group 17 atom needs just one electron to reach the noble-gas configuration, whereas nitrogen in Group 15 needs three. Chlorine therefore accepts electrons far more readily than nitrogen, giving \(\text{F} > \text{O} > \text{Cl} > \text{N}\).
